Morality Play. A morality play is a medieval and early modern theatrical form in which abstract virtues and vices—Charity, Despair, Greed, Conscience—are personified as characters who struggle for the soul of a human protagonist, usually called Everyman or Mankind. These plays were didactic allegories staging the Christian battle for salvation, and they bridge medieval mystery plays and modern drama by pioneering the individual as the focus of moral action rather than biblical spectacle.

The form flourished from the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, primarily in England and France. The plays were performed in towns and courtyards, appealing to general audiences, not just the clergy. The dramatic structure consists of a protagonist representing humanity who is tempted by Vice, aided by Virtue, and guided by figures like Conscience or Good Deeds toward salvation or damnation. The outcome is never certain until the end. Characters have names like Everyman, Good Deeds, Strength, Knowledge, Gluttony, Sloth—making moral psychology visible and tangible on stage through abstract personification.

Everyman, dating from around fourteen ninety-five, is the most famous example and only complete survivor. Its protagonist must account for his life before God after Death summons him. Companions abandon him except Good Deeds. The moral urgency is distinct from mystery plays, which retell biblical narrative. Morality plays stage the present spiritual crisis of each viewer—your soul is on trial, now, as you watch. The plays mix serious theology with crude humor and slapstick Vice-characters, making moral doctrine accessible and memorable through laughter and spectacle. Comic and tragic elements interweave.

Morality plays had influence on Renaissance drama. The interplay of Vice and Virtue anticipated the psychological complexity of Shakespeare's villains—Iago, Edmund—and the introspective protagonists of tragedy. Everyman is the canonical morality play, the most complete surviving text and model for the genre. Medieval drama encompasses the mystery and miracle play tradition, with morality plays as the late flowering, updated for moral rather than biblical focus. Allegory is the governing technique—abstract concepts embodied as speaking characters to teach moral truth. The period of late medieval drama was when morality plays dominated, bridging toward Renaissance theater. Death and mortality are the themes that haunt morality plays. The sudden reckoning with mortality and judgment drive the action. Christianity is the theological framework. Salvation and damnation, virtue and sin, are the stakes of every play. The Vice is a theatrical creation of morality plays—proto-villains who entertain while corrupting.
